# Unit 3: The digestive system

INC Unit III (6 hours): structure of the alimentary canal and the accessory organs of digestion, with nursing applications. Digestive juices and absorption are covered in Applied Physiology.

## 3.1 Overview

```text
ALIMENTARY CANAL (a continuous tube; lengths quoted in textbooks vary with muscle tone)
Mouth → Pharynx → Oesophagus → Stomach → Small intestine (duodenum, jejunum, ileum)
      → Large intestine (caecum + appendix, colon, rectum) → Anal canal → Anus

ACCESSORY ORGANS
Teeth, tongue, salivary glands, liver, gallbladder (biliary tract), pancreas
```

## 3.2 General structure of the wall of the alimentary canal

From the oesophagus to the anal canal the wall has four layers.

| Layer (inside → out) | Structure | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mucosa | Epithelium, lamina propria (loose connective tissue with lymphoid tissue), thin muscularis mucosae | Stratified squamous in mouth, oesophagus and anal canal (wear and tear); simple columnar from stomach to rectum (secretion and absorption) |
| Submucosa | Loose connective tissue with blood vessels, lymphatics and the **submucosal (Meissner's) nerve plexus** | Controls secretion |
| Muscularis externa | Inner circular and outer longitudinal smooth muscle with the **myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus** between them | Peristalsis; the stomach has an extra inner oblique layer |
| Serosa / adventitia | Visceral peritoneum (serosa) in the abdomen; loose connective tissue (adventitia) where there is no peritoneum, as in most of the oesophagus | Reduces friction |

**Sphincters** are thickened rings of circular muscle: upper and lower oesophageal, pyloric, ileocaecal, internal anal (smooth, involuntary) and external anal (skeletal, voluntary).

**Peritoneum**: the large serous membrane of the abdomen. Parietal peritoneum lines the wall; visceral peritoneum covers organs. Folds include the **mesentery** (holds the small intestine, carries its vessels), the **greater omentum** (apron hanging from the stomach over the intestines, stores fat and walls off infection) and the **lesser omentum** (stomach to liver). Organs behind the peritoneum are **retroperitoneal** — kidneys, pancreas (mostly), most of the duodenum, ascending and descending colon.

## 3.3 The mouth (oral cavity)

- Bounded by the lips in front, cheeks at the sides, **hard palate** (maxilla and palatine bones) and **soft palate** above, tongue and floor below; opens behind into the oropharynx. The **uvula** hangs from the soft palate; during swallowing the soft palate rises to close the nasopharynx.
- **Tongue**: skeletal muscle covered with mucous membrane; attached to the hyoid bone and floor of the mouth by the frenulum. The upper surface has papillae (filiform, fungiform, circumvallate) carrying taste buds. Motor nerve: hypoglossal (XII).
- **Teeth**: two sets.

| Set | Number | Per quadrant |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Deciduous (milk) teeth | 20 | 2 incisors, 1 canine, 2 molars |
| Permanent teeth | 32 | 2 incisors, 1 canine, 2 premolars, 3 molars |

A tooth has a **crown** (above the gum), **neck** and **root** (in the socket). Layers: **enamel** (hardest substance in the body) over the crown, **dentine** under it, **pulp cavity** with vessels and nerves in the centre, and **cementum** covering the root. The periodontal ligament holds the tooth in the socket.

## 3.4 Salivary glands

| Gland | Location | Duct | Secretion |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Parotid (largest) | In front of and below the ear | **Stensen's (parotid) duct**, opens opposite the upper second molar | Watery (serous) |
| Submandibular | Under the lower jaw | **Wharton's duct**, opens beside the frenulum of the tongue | Mixed |
| Sublingual (smallest) | Under the tongue in the floor of mouth | Many small ducts | Mainly mucous |

Mumps is a viral infection of the parotid glands.

## 3.5 Oesophagus

- Muscular tube about **25 cm long**, from the pharynx at C6 through the thorax (behind the trachea and heart), passing through the diaphragm at **T10**, to the stomach (cardiac orifice at about T11).
- Muscle: skeletal in the upper third, mixed in the middle, smooth in the lower third.
- Lining: stratified squamous non-keratinised epithelium.
- The **lower oesophageal (cardiac) sphincter** prevents reflux of stomach acid; weakness leads to heartburn (GERD).
- Normally narrowed at four places (start, crossing of aortic arch, crossing of left bronchus, passing through diaphragm); swallowed objects and tubes may catch here.

## 3.6 Stomach

J-shaped, widest part of the canal, in the epigastric, left hypochondriac and umbilical regions, under the diaphragm.

```text
            Fundus
           ______
  Cardiac /      \
 orifice |        \   Greater curvature
  Lesser |  Body   |
curvature \         \
           \_Antrum__\__ Pylorus → Pyloric sphincter → Duodenum
```

- **Parts**: cardia, fundus (above the level of the cardiac orifice; often contains gas), body, pyloric antrum, pyloric canal and **pyloric sphincter**.
- **Curvatures**: lesser (right/upper, lesser omentum attached) and greater (left/lower, greater omentum attached).
- **Muscle**: three layers — outer longitudinal, middle circular, **inner oblique** (for churning).
- **Rugae**: folds of mucosa when empty; flatten as the stomach fills (capacity about 1.5 litres in an adult, varies).
- **Gastric glands** (in gastric pits): **mucous cells** (mucus), **chief (peptic) cells** (pepsinogen), **parietal (oxyntic) cells** (hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor, needed for vitamin B12 absorption), **G cells** in the antrum (gastrin).

## 3.7 Small intestine

About 5–6 m long (often quoted; varies), from the pyloric sphincter to the ileocaecal valve. Main site of digestion and absorption.

| Part | Length (approximate) | Features |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Duodenum | 25 cm | C-shaped around the head of the pancreas; mostly retroperitoneal; the common bile duct and main pancreatic duct open together at the **hepatopancreatic ampulla (ampulla of Vater)** on the major duodenal papilla, guarded by the **sphincter of Oddi**; **Brunner's glands** secrete alkaline mucus |
| Jejunum | About 2/5 of the rest | Thicker wall, wider, more vascular, prominent circular folds |
| Ileum | About 3/5 of the rest | Thinner wall, fewer folds, many **Peyer's patches** (lymphoid tissue); ends at the ileocaecal valve |

**Adaptations for absorption** (increase surface area):

1. **Circular folds (plicae circulares)** of mucosa and submucosa.
2. **Villi**: finger-like projections, each with a capillary network and a central lymph vessel (**lacteal**) that absorbs fat.
3. **Microvilli** on the epithelial cells (brush border).
4. **Intestinal glands (crypts of Lieberkühn)** between villi secrete intestinal juice.

```text
   Villus (section)
      /\        epithelium with microvilli
     /  \       goblet cells
    | ┃  |      ┃ = lacteal (fat → lymph)
    |~┃~ |      ~ = capillary network (sugars, amino acids → portal blood)
   _|_┃__|_
     crypt
```

## 3.8 Large intestine

About 1.5 m long, from the ileocaecal valve to the anus; wider than the small intestine.

- **Caecum**: blind pouch in the right iliac fossa; the **vermiform appendix** (about 8–9 cm, rich in lymphoid tissue) hangs from it. McBurney's point (one-third of the way from the right ASIS to the umbilicus) marks the usual base of the appendix.
- **Colon**: ascending (right side, up to the hepatic flexure), transverse (across the abdomen, to the splenic flexure), descending (left side), sigmoid (S-shaped, in the pelvis).
- **Rectum**: about 12–13 cm, in front of the sacrum.
- **Anal canal**: about 4 cm; internal sphincter (smooth, involuntary) and external sphincter (skeletal, voluntary, pudendal nerve).
- **Special features of the colon**: longitudinal muscle in three bands (**taeniae coli**), which pucker the wall into pouches (**haustra**); small fat tags (**appendices epiploicae**). No villi; many goblet cells.

## 3.9 Liver

- Largest gland of the body, about **1.5 kg** in adults; lies mainly in the right hypochondriac and epigastric regions under the diaphragm, protected by the lower ribs.
- **Lobes**: large right and smaller left (separated in front by the falciform ligament), plus the small caudate and quadrate lobes on the under (visceral) surface.
- **Porta hepatis** (on the under surface): entry of the **hepatic artery** (oxygenated blood, about one-quarter of the supply) and **portal vein** (nutrient-rich blood from the gut and spleen, about three-quarters); exit of the right and left hepatic ducts. Blood leaves through the **hepatic veins** into the inferior vena cava.
- Covered by a fibrous capsule; most of it by peritoneum.

**Microscopic structure — the hepatic lobule**: a roughly hexagonal unit with a **central vein** in the middle. Plates of liver cells (hepatocytes) radiate from it, separated by **sinusoids** (lined by Kupffer cells — macrophages). At the corners are **portal triads**: a branch of the hepatic artery, a branch of the portal vein and a bile ductule. Blood flows from the corners to the central vein; bile flows the opposite way, through canaliculi to the bile ducts.

## 3.10 Gallbladder and biliary tract

- **Gallbladder**: pear-shaped sac (fundus, body, neck) under the right lobe of the liver; stores and concentrates bile (capacity about 30–50 ml). Its fundus lies near the tip of the right 9th costal cartilage.
- **Ducts**:

```text
Right hepatic duct + Left hepatic duct → Common hepatic duct
Common hepatic duct + Cystic duct (from gallbladder) → Common bile duct
Common bile duct + Main pancreatic duct → Ampulla of Vater → Duodenum (2nd part)
```

A stone blocking the common bile duct stops bile reaching the gut, causing jaundice and pale stools.

## 3.11 Pancreas

- Soft, lobulated gland about 12–15 cm long, lying across the back of the upper abdomen behind the stomach (retroperitoneal). Parts: **head** (in the curve of the duodenum), neck, **body** and **tail** (reaching the spleen).
- **Exocrine part** (about 98–99%): acini secrete digestive enzymes into the main pancreatic duct (duct of Wirsung), which joins the common bile duct; an accessory duct (of Santorini) may also open into the duodenum.
- **Endocrine part**: the **islets of Langerhans** (see Unit 5) secrete insulin and glucagon into the blood.

## 3.12 Blood and nerve supply in brief

- Arteries from the abdominal aorta: **coeliac trunk** (stomach, liver, spleen, pancreas, upper duodenum), **superior mesenteric artery** (small intestine to the first two-thirds of the transverse colon), **inferior mesenteric artery** (rest of the colon and upper rectum).
- Veins from the gut and spleen join to form the **hepatic portal vein**, so absorbed food and drugs pass through the liver before reaching the general circulation (first-pass effect).
- Nerves: parasympathetic (vagus nerve and pelvic splanchnic nerves) increases movement and secretion; sympathetic reduces them.

## 3.13 Application and implication in nursing

- **Nasogastric tube**: measured from the nose tip to the earlobe and then to the xiphisternum (NEX measurement); passes the natural narrowings of the oesophagus. Confirm position before every feed as per hospital policy.
- **Oral care**: the mouth harbours many microbes; good oral hygiene prevents infection of the parotid gland (parotitis) and chest infection in unconscious patients.
- **Abdominal assessment** uses the regions and quadrants: RLQ tenderness at McBurney's point suggests appendicitis; RUQ pain may be from the gallbladder or liver.
- **Enema and suppository** insertion follow the direction of the rectum and anal canal; the patient lies in the left lateral position, which follows the curve of the sigmoid colon and rectum.
- **Liver biopsy and paracentesis** require knowledge of liver position and the peritoneal cavity.
- The ileum absorbs vitamin B12 and bile salts; patients who lose the ileum or lack intrinsic factor need monitoring for B12 deficiency.
- Stoma care: a colostomy (from colon) gives formed stool; an ileostomy gives liquid, irritant output that needs careful skin protection.

## Remember

- Four layers of the gut wall: mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa, serosa/adventitia.
- Permanent teeth 32, deciduous 20; enamel is the hardest substance.
- Parotid duct opens opposite the upper second molar.
- Oesophagus 25 cm, passes the diaphragm at T10; stomach has an extra oblique muscle layer.
- Parietal cells: HCl and intrinsic factor; chief cells: pepsinogen.
- Duodenum: ampulla of Vater, sphincter of Oddi, Brunner's glands. Ileum: Peyer's patches.
- Villi with lacteals absorb fat.
- Colon: taeniae coli, haustra, appendices epiploicae.
- Liver: hepatic artery + portal vein in, hepatic veins out; lobule with central vein and portal triads.
- Cystic duct + common hepatic duct = common bile duct.
- Pancreas: exocrine acini + endocrine islets.

# Unit 4: The circulatory and lymphatic system

INC Unit IV (6 hours): blood components, arterial and venous systems, the heart (position, chambers, layers, valves, coronary arteries, nerve and blood supply), lymphatic tissue and the veins used for IV injections. Heart function, blood pressure and blood clotting are in Applied Physiology.

## 4.1 Blood components (structure)

Blood is a fluid connective tissue, about 5 litres in an adult (roughly 7–8% of body weight).

| Component | Share of blood | Structure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Plasma | About 55% | Pale yellow fluid: about 90% water with proteins (albumin, globulins, fibrinogen), salts, nutrients, hormones, wastes |
| Red blood cells (erythrocytes) | About 45% of the volume (haematocrit) | Biconcave discs about 7–8 µm across, **no nucleus**, packed with haemoglobin; flexible enough to squeeze through capillaries |
| White blood cells (leucocytes) | Under 1% | Nucleated cells of five kinds (below) |
| Platelets (thrombocytes) | Under 1% | Small cell fragments without a nucleus, from megakaryocytes in the bone marrow |

| White cell | Group | Nucleus | Main role |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Neutrophil (most common) | Granulocyte | 3–5 lobes | Phagocytosis of bacteria |
| Eosinophil | Granulocyte | 2 lobes, red granules | Allergy, parasites |
| Basophil (least common) | Granulocyte | S-shaped, dark blue granules | Releases histamine and heparin |
| Lymphocyte | Agranulocyte | Large round nucleus filling the cell | Immunity (B and T cells) |
| Monocyte (largest) | Agranulocyte | Kidney- or horseshoe-shaped | Becomes a macrophage in tissues |

All blood cells are made in the **red bone marrow** (in adults: flat bones, vertebrae, ribs, sternum, pelvis, ends of long bones).

## 4.2 Blood vessels: structure

All vessels except capillaries have three coats (tunicae).

| Coat | Structure |
| --- | --- |
| Tunica intima (inner) | Endothelium (simple squamous) on a thin connective tissue layer |
| Tunica media (middle) | Smooth muscle and elastic fibres |
| Tunica adventitia / externa (outer) | Connective tissue with small vessels (vasa vasorum) and nerves |

| Feature | Artery | Vein | Capillary |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Direction | Away from the heart | Towards the heart | Between arterioles and venules |
| Wall | Thick, muscular and elastic | Thin, less muscle | One layer of endothelium only |
| Lumen | Narrow, round | Wide, often collapsed | About the width of one red cell |
| Valves | None (except at the heart outflow) | Present in limb veins | None |
| Pressure | High; pulsatile | Low | Low |
| Bleeding when cut | Spurting bright red | Steady flow, darker | Oozing |

- **Elastic (conducting) arteries**: aorta and its main branches; stretch and recoil.
- **Muscular (distributing) arteries**: radial, femoral; control flow to organs.
- **Arterioles**: control blood pressure by narrowing and widening.
- **Venous valves** are folds of intima; they stop backflow. When they fail, varicose veins develop.

## 4.3 The arterial system

```text
Left ventricle → Ascending aorta (gives right and left coronary arteries)
   → Arch of aorta: 1. Brachiocephalic trunk → right common carotid + right subclavian
                    2. Left common carotid
                    3. Left subclavian
   → Descending thoracic aorta (intercostal, bronchial, oesophageal branches)
   → Abdominal aorta (from T12): coeliac trunk, superior mesenteric, renal, gonadal,
                                  inferior mesenteric, lumbar arteries
   → divides at L4 into right and left common iliac arteries
        → internal iliac (pelvis) + external iliac → femoral artery (lower limb)
```

- **Common carotid** → external carotid (face, scalp) and internal carotid (brain, eye).
- **Subclavian** → axillary → **brachial** (in front of the elbow) → **radial** and **ulnar** (forearm and hand). The subclavian also gives the **vertebral artery** to the brain.
- **Femoral** → popliteal (behind knee) → anterior tibial (→ **dorsalis pedis**) and posterior tibial.
- **Circle of Willis**: ring of arteries at the base of the brain joining the internal carotid and vertebral (basilar) systems, so blockage of one vessel can be partly compensated.

**Pulse points**: temporal, carotid (side of the neck, beside the trachea), brachial (medial to the biceps tendon at the elbow), radial (lateral wrist, thumb side), femoral (groin, midway between ASIS and symphysis pubis), popliteal, posterior tibial (behind the medial malleolus), dorsalis pedis (top of the foot), apical (5th left intercostal space, midclavicular line).

## 4.4 The venous system

- **Systemic veins** return blood to the right atrium through the **superior vena cava** (head, neck, upper limbs, thorax) and **inferior vena cava** (abdomen, pelvis, lower limbs), and the coronary sinus (heart wall).
- Head: internal jugular vein (from the brain via the dural venous sinuses) and external jugular vein; internal jugular + subclavian = brachiocephalic vein; right and left brachiocephalic veins = superior vena cava.
- Limbs have **superficial veins** (in the subcutaneous tissue, visible, used for injections) and **deep veins** (running with arteries, sharing their names).
- **Hepatic portal system**: veins from the stomach, intestines, pancreas and spleen join to form the portal vein, which carries blood to the liver before it reaches the inferior vena cava.

## 4.5 Veins used for IV injections

**Upper limb (first choice in adults)**

```text
   Hand: dorsal venous network (back of hand)
          |                         |
    Cephalic vein (lateral,     Basilic vein (medial,
    thumb side)                 little-finger side)
          \                         /
           \__ Median cubital vein _/   ← in front of the elbow (cubital fossa)
```

| Vein | Where | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dorsal metacarpal veins / dorsal venous network | Back of hand | Peripheral cannulation |
| Cephalic vein | Lateral (thumb side) of forearm and arm | Cannulation; large and straight |
| Basilic vein | Medial side of forearm and arm | Cannulation; PICC lines |
| Median cubital vein | Front of the elbow | Most common for **venepuncture** (blood samples) |
| Median antebrachial vein | Front of forearm | Alternative site |

**Other sites**

- Lower limb: **great saphenous vein** (in front of the medial malleolus, runs up the medial leg) and dorsal venous arch of the foot — used when arm veins are not available (higher risk of thrombosis in adults).
- Neck: **external jugular vein** (emergency).
- Central veins: internal jugular, subclavian and femoral veins for central venous catheters (placed by trained staff).
- Infants: scalp veins and hand/foot veins.

Choose distal sites first so the vein above remains usable later, avoid joints when possible, avoid the arm with a fistula or on the side of a mastectomy with lymph node removal, and avoid veins that are hard, inflamed or near an infected area.

## 4.6 The heart: position and relations

- A hollow muscular organ about the size of the owner's closed fist (about 250–350 g), lying in the **middle mediastinum** between the lungs, behind the sternum.
- About two-thirds of it lies to the left of the midline.
- **Apex**: points down, forward and to the left; lies at the **left 5th intercostal space, just medial to the midclavicular line** (about 9 cm from the midline in adults) — the apex beat.
- **Base**: faces backward and upward (mainly the left atrium), at about the level of T5–T8 in the lying position; the great vessels attach here.

| Relation | Structure |
| --- | --- |
| In front | Sternum, costal cartilages, thymus remnant |
| Behind | Oesophagus, descending aorta, vertebrae (T5–T8) |
| Sides | Lungs and pleura; phrenic nerves |
| Below | Diaphragm (central tendon) |
| Above | Great vessels: aorta, pulmonary trunk, superior vena cava |

## 4.7 Layers of the heart

```text
 Outside → inside
 Fibrous pericardium      (tough outer sac, attached to the diaphragm)
 Serous pericardium:
    Parietal layer        (lines the fibrous sac)
    — Pericardial cavity with a little serous fluid —
    Visceral layer = Epicardium (on the heart surface)
 Myocardium               (cardiac muscle; thickest in the left ventricle)
 Endocardium              (endothelium lining the chambers and covering the valves)
```

- Fluid between the layers of serous pericardium reduces friction. Fluid or blood collecting here can squeeze the heart (cardiac tamponade).
- The myocardium of the left ventricle is about three times thicker than that of the right, because it pumps blood around the whole body.

## 4.8 Chambers of the heart

Four chambers: two atria (receiving) and two ventricles (pumping). The right and left sides are separated by the **interatrial septum** (has the fossa ovalis, remnant of the fetal foramen ovale) and **interventricular septum**.

| Chamber | Receives from | Sends to | Features |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Right atrium | Superior and inferior venae cavae, coronary sinus | Right ventricle | Contains the SA node; has an ear-like auricle |
| Right ventricle | Right atrium | Pulmonary trunk → lungs | Trabeculae carneae, papillary muscles, chordae tendineae |
| Left atrium | Four pulmonary veins | Left ventricle | Forms most of the base |
| Left ventricle | Left atrium | Aorta → body | Thickest wall; forms the apex |

```text
 Body → SVC/IVC → RA → tricuspid → RV → pulmonary valve → pulmonary arteries → lungs
 Lungs → 4 pulmonary veins → LA → mitral → LV → aortic valve → aorta → body
```

## 4.9 Heart valves

| Valve | Position | Cusps |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tricuspid (right atrioventricular) | Right atrium → right ventricle | 3 |
| Mitral (bicuspid, left atrioventricular) | Left atrium → left ventricle | 2 |
| Pulmonary (semilunar) | Right ventricle → pulmonary trunk | 3 half-moon cusps |
| Aortic (semilunar) | Left ventricle → aorta | 3 half-moon cusps; coronary arteries arise just above two of them |

- Atrioventricular valves are held by **chordae tendineae** attached to **papillary muscles**, which stop the cusps turning inside out when the ventricles contract.
- Closure of the AV valves gives the first heart sound ("lub"); closure of the semilunar valves gives the second ("dub").
- Auscultation areas (where each valve is best heard, not where it lies): aortic — right 2nd intercostal space at the sternal edge; pulmonary — left 2nd intercostal space; tricuspid — lower left sternal edge (4th–5th space); mitral — apex (left 5th intercostal space, midclavicular line).

## 4.10 Coronary arteries (blood supply of the heart)

The heart muscle gets its own blood from the **right and left coronary arteries**, which arise from the ascending aorta just above the aortic valve. They fill mainly when the ventricles relax (diastole).

| Artery | Branches | Supplies (usual pattern) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Right coronary artery (RCA) | Marginal branch, posterior interventricular (descending) branch in most people | Right atrium, right ventricle, back of the septum, SA node (in most) and AV node (in most) |
| Left coronary artery (LCA) | **Left anterior descending (anterior interventricular)** and **circumflex** | Left atrium, most of the left ventricle, front two-thirds of the septum |

Venous blood from the heart wall drains mainly through cardiac veins into the **coronary sinus**, which opens into the right atrium. Blocking a coronary artery causes myocardial infarction (heart attack) in the area it supplies; the left anterior descending artery is commonly involved.

## 4.11 Nerve supply and conducting system

- **Sympathetic** nerves (from the upper thoracic segments) increase heart rate and force.
- **Parasympathetic** supply through the **vagus nerve** slows the heart.
- These act through the cardiac plexus; they adjust, but do not start, the heartbeat.
- **Conducting system** (specialised cardiac muscle that starts and spreads the impulse):

```text
SA node (right atrium wall, near SVC opening — the pacemaker)
   → atrial muscle → AV node (lower interatrial septum)
   → Bundle of His → right and left bundle branches (in the septum)
   → Purkinje fibres (ventricle walls)
```

## 4.12 The lymphatic system

**Lymph** is tissue fluid that has entered lymph vessels; it is clear, or milky (chyle) after a fatty meal from the gut.

- **Lymph capillaries**: blind-ended, very permeable; absent from the CNS, bone marrow and cartilage.
- **Lymph vessels**: like thin veins with many valves; carry lymph through lymph nodes.
- **Lymph ducts**:
  - **Thoracic duct** (largest, about 40 cm): begins at the **cisterna chyli** in the abdomen, drains the lower limbs, abdomen, left side of the thorax, left arm and left side of the head and neck; empties into the junction of the **left subclavian and left internal jugular veins**.
  - **Right lymphatic duct**: drains the right arm and right side of the head, neck and thorax into the right subclavian/internal jugular junction.

**Lymphatic tissue and organs**

| Organ | Structure | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lymph nodes | Bean-shaped, capsule, cortex with follicles (B cells), paracortex (T cells), medulla; several afferent vessels in, one efferent vessel out at the hilum | Filter lymph; groups in neck (cervical), axilla, groin (inguinal), around abdominal vessels |
| Spleen | Largest lymphatic organ, left hypochondrium behind ribs 9–11; white pulp (lymphoid) and red pulp (blood-filled sinusoids) | Removes old red cells; stores platelets; immune responses. Injury causes heavy bleeding |
| Thymus | Behind the sternum in the upper mediastinum; large in children, shrinks after puberty | T-lymphocytes mature here |
| Tonsils | Palatine, pharyngeal (adenoids), lingual — a ring of lymphoid tissue in the pharynx | Guard the entry to the respiratory and digestive tracts |
| MALT | Lymphoid tissue in mucosa, e.g. Peyer's patches, appendix | Local immunity |

## 4.13 Application and implication in nursing

- IV cannulation and venepuncture depend on knowing the dorsal venous network, cephalic, basilic and median cubital veins; avoid arteries (the brachial artery lies deep to the median cubital region).
- Pulse is felt where an artery crosses a bone near the surface; the radial pulse is routine, the carotid is used in collapse.
- Chest compressions over the lower half of the sternum squeeze the heart between the sternum and vertebral column.
- Valves in leg veins plus muscle pumping return blood; immobility allows stasis and deep vein thrombosis, so early ambulation and leg exercises are taught.
- Lymph nodes are examined for infection and cancer spread; after axillary node removal the arm on that side may swell (lymphoedema), so it is not used for BP, injections or cannulation unless policy allows.
- Splenic injury from trauma to the left lower ribs can cause internal bleeding — watch vital signs.

## Remember

- RBC: biconcave, no nucleus; neutrophils most, basophils fewest; monocyte largest.
- Arteries thick muscular wall; veins have valves; capillaries are one cell thick.
- Arch of aorta: brachiocephalic, left common carotid, left subclavian.
- Median cubital vein = venepuncture; cephalic lateral, basilic medial.
- Apex beat: left 5th intercostal space, midclavicular line.
- Layers: pericardium, myocardium, endocardium.
- Mitral = bicuspid (left); tricuspid on the right.
- Coronary arteries arise from the ascending aorta; drain to the coronary sinus.
- SA node is the pacemaker; vagus slows the heart.
- Thoracic duct drains most of the body into the left venous angle.

# Unit 5: The endocrine system and the sensory organs

This notes file joins two small INC units: **Unit V, the endocrine system** (4 hours: structure of the hypothalamus, pineal, pituitary, thyroid, parathyroid, thymus, pancreas and adrenal glands) and **Unit VI, the sensory organs** (4 hours: structure of the skin, eye, ear, nose and tongue). Hormone actions and the physiology of vision and hearing belong to Applied Physiology; only the hormone names are listed here so the structure makes sense.

## Part A — The endocrine system

## 5.1 Endocrine glands in general

Endocrine glands are **ductless**; they release hormones directly into the blood, so they have a very rich capillary supply.

```text
             Pineal gland (brain)
             Hypothalamus + Pituitary (base of brain)
             Thyroid + Parathyroids (neck)
             Thymus (upper mediastinum)
             Adrenal glands (on top of kidneys)
             Pancreatic islets (abdomen)
             Ovaries / Testes (pelvis / scrotum)
```

## 5.2 Hypothalamus

- Part of the diencephalon, below the thalamus, forming the floor and lower side walls of the third ventricle.
- Connected to the pituitary by the **infundibulum (pituitary stalk)**.
- Contains groups of nerve cells (nuclei), e.g. supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei, which make ADH and oxytocin.
- Links the nervous and endocrine systems through:
  - **Nerve fibres** (hypothalamo-hypophyseal tract) to the posterior pituitary.
  - **Hypophyseal portal veins** carrying releasing and inhibiting hormones to the anterior pituitary.

## 5.3 Pituitary gland (hypophysis)

- Pea-sized (about 1 cm, 0.5 g), lies in the **sella turcica (hypophyseal fossa) of the sphenoid bone**, below the optic chiasma. Called the "master gland".

| Lobe | Origin and structure | Hormones released |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Anterior (adenohypophysis) | Glandular epithelium from the roof of the embryonic mouth; receives hypothalamic hormones by the portal veins | GH, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH, prolactin |
| Posterior (neurohypophysis) | Nervous tissue, an extension of the hypothalamus; nerve fibres and pituicytes | Stores and releases ADH and oxytocin (made in the hypothalamus) |

Because the optic chiasma lies just above, a pituitary tumour can press on it and cause loss of the outer halves of the visual fields.

## 5.4 Pineal gland

- Small cone-shaped body (about 8 mm) attached to the roof of the third ventricle, behind the hypothalamus.
- Made of pinealocytes and neuroglia; often contains calcium deposits ("brain sand") in adults, visible on X-ray.
- Secretes **melatonin**, linked to the sleep–wake cycle.

## 5.5 Thyroid gland

- Butterfly-shaped gland in the front of the neck, at the level of C5–T1, weighing about 25 g.
- **Two lateral lobes** on either side of the trachea and larynx, joined by an **isthmus** across the 2nd–4th tracheal rings; sometimes a pyramidal lobe rises from the isthmus.
- Enclosed in a capsule; moves up with swallowing because it is attached to the larynx.
- **Microscopic structure**: many **follicles** lined by cuboidal follicular cells, filled with colloid (thyroglobulin). Follicular cells make **T3 and T4**. Between follicles are **parafollicular (C) cells**, which make **calcitonin**.
- Blood supply: superior thyroid artery (external carotid) and inferior thyroid artery (thyrocervical trunk of subclavian). The **recurrent laryngeal nerves** run close behind the gland.
- Enlargement of the gland is a goitre.

## 5.6 Parathyroid glands

- Usually **four** tiny glands (about the size of a rice grain), two on the back of each thyroid lobe (superior and inferior pairs).
- Chief cells secrete **parathormone (PTH)**, which raises blood calcium.
- They can be removed or damaged by accident in thyroid surgery, causing low calcium (tingling, tetany). Nurses watch for this after thyroidectomy.

## 5.7 Thymus

- Two-lobed lymphoid organ behind the sternum in the upper (superior) mediastinum, in front of the great vessels.
- Large in childhood; after puberty it is gradually replaced by fat (involution).
- Each lobule has an outer **cortex** packed with developing T-lymphocytes and an inner **medulla** with **Hassall's corpuscles**.
- Hormone: **thymosin**, which helps T-cell maturation.

## 5.8 Pancreas (endocrine part)

- The pancreas (structure in Unit 3) has about one million **islets of Langerhans** scattered among the exocrine acini, more in the tail.

| Cell | Proportion | Hormone |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Alpha (α) | About 20% | Glucagon |
| Beta (β) | About 70% (the majority) | Insulin |
| Delta (δ) | Small | Somatostatin |
| PP (F) cells | Few | Pancreatic polypeptide |

## 5.9 Adrenal (suprarenal) glands

- Two glands, one on the upper pole of each kidney, inside the renal fascia. The right is triangular (pyramid-like); the left is crescent (semilunar) shaped.
- Each has an outer **cortex** and an inner **medulla**, which are really two different glands.

```text
 Capsule
 Cortex: Zona glomerulosa    → mineralocorticoids (aldosterone)      "Salt"
         Zona fasciculata    → glucocorticoids (cortisol)            "Sugar"
         Zona reticularis    → sex hormones (androgens)              "Sex"
 Medulla (chromaffin cells, modified sympathetic nerve cells)
                             → adrenaline and noradrenaline
```

(Memory: "GFR — Salt, Sugar, Sex" from outside in.)

- The medulla is supplied by sympathetic preganglionic fibres; it acts like a sympathetic ganglion.

## Part B — The sensory organs

## 5.10 Skin

The skin is the largest organ (about 1.5–2 m² in adults). Two main layers sit on the subcutaneous tissue.

**Epidermis** — stratified squamous keratinised epithelium, **no blood vessels**. Layers from deep to surface:

| Layer | Features |
| --- | --- |
| Stratum basale (germinativum) | One layer of dividing cells; melanocytes (pigment) present here |
| Stratum spinosum | Several layers joined by desmosomes ("prickle cells") |
| Stratum granulosum | Cells with keratin granules, starting to die |
| Stratum lucidum | Clear layer, only in thick skin (palms, soles) |
| Stratum corneum | Flat dead keratin-filled cells that flake off |

**Dermis** — dense connective tissue with collagen and elastic fibres, blood vessels, lymphatics, nerves and sensory receptors, hair follicles, sweat and sebaceous glands.

- **Papillary layer** (upper): dermal papillae (fingerprints), Meissner's corpuscles (light touch).
- **Reticular layer** (deeper): strong fibres; Pacinian corpuscles (pressure, vibration) are in the deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue.

**Appendages**: hair (shaft, root, follicle, arrector pili muscle), nails, **sebaceous glands** (open into hair follicles; sebum), **sweat glands** — eccrine (all over, open on the skin surface) and apocrine (axilla, groin; open into hair follicles).

**Subcutaneous tissue (hypodermis)**: loose areolar and adipose tissue — the layer used for subcutaneous injections.

```text
 Surface ────────────────── stratum corneum
 EPIDERMIS  (no vessels)    ...stratum basale
 ─────────── dermal papillae ───────────
 DERMIS: vessels, nerves, sweat gland, sebaceous gland, hair follicle
 ────────────────────────────────────────
 SUBCUTANEOUS: fat, larger vessels
```

## 5.11 Eye

The eyeball (about 2.5 cm across) lies in the bony **orbit**, cushioned by fat. Accessory structures: eyebrows, eyelids, conjunctiva, lacrimal apparatus, six extrinsic eye muscles.

**Three coats of the eyeball**

| Coat | Parts | Features |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Outer fibrous | **Sclera** (white, back 5/6) and **cornea** (transparent, front 1/6) | Cornea has no blood vessels; bends light most; very sensitive (corneal reflex) |
| Middle vascular (uvea) | **Choroid**, **ciliary body**, **iris** | Choroid is pigmented and vascular; ciliary body has ciliary muscle (changes lens shape) and makes aqueous humour; iris has a central opening, the **pupil**, with sphincter and dilator pupillae muscles |
| Inner nervous | **Retina** | Rods (dim light) and cones (colour, detail); **macula lutea** with the **fovea centralis** (sharpest vision, cones only); **optic disc** (blind spot, no receptors) where the optic nerve leaves |

**Contents**

- **Lens**: transparent, biconvex, held by suspensory ligaments (zonules) from the ciliary body. Clouding = cataract.
- **Aqueous humour**: watery fluid in the front of the eye (anterior and posterior chambers), made by the ciliary body, drained through the canal of Schlemm. Poor drainage raises pressure (glaucoma).
- **Vitreous humour (body)**: jelly behind the lens, keeps the eyeball shape.

```text
         Cornea
   Anterior chamber (aqueous)
    Iris ─ pupil ─ Iris
         Lens
   Vitreous body
   Retina  ── Fovea ── Optic disc → Optic nerve
   (Choroid and sclera outside)
```

**Accessory structures**

- **Conjunctiva**: thin mucous membrane lining the eyelids and covering the white of the eye (not the cornea).
- **Lacrimal apparatus**: lacrimal gland (upper outer part of the orbit) → tears flow across the eye → puncta at the inner corner → canaliculi → lacrimal sac → **nasolacrimal duct** → inferior meatus of the nose.
- Extrinsic muscles: four recti (superior, inferior, medial, lateral) and two obliques. Nerves: lateral rectus — abducens (VI); superior oblique — trochlear (IV); all others — oculomotor (III).

## 5.12 Ear

```text
 EXTERNAL EAR         | MIDDLE EAR                    | INNER EAR
 Pinna → External     | Tympanic cavity with ossicles | Cochlea (hearing)
 acoustic meatus →    | Malleus → Incus → Stapes →    | Vestibule + semicircular
 Tympanic membrane    | oval window                   | canals (balance)
                      | Auditory tube → nasopharynx   | → Vestibulocochlear nerve (VIII)
```

- **External ear**: pinna (elastic cartilage covered with skin) and the **external acoustic meatus** (about 2.5 cm, S-shaped; outer third cartilage, inner two-thirds bone; ceruminous glands make wax). Ends at the **tympanic membrane (eardrum)**, a thin, pearly grey membrane.
- **Middle ear (tympanic cavity)**: air-filled space in the temporal bone with the three smallest bones of the body — **malleus** (attached to the eardrum), **incus**, **stapes** (footplate in the oval window). The **auditory (Eustachian) tube** connects it to the nasopharynx and equalises pressure. It also connects behind with the mastoid air cells.
- **Inner ear (labyrinth)**: a bony labyrinth filled with perilymph, containing a membranous labyrinth filled with endolymph.
  - **Cochlea**: snail-shaped tube (about 2¾ turns) containing the **organ of Corti** — the hearing receptor.
  - **Vestibule** (utricle and saccule) and three **semicircular canals** — balance and head position.

## 5.13 Nose (organ of smell)

- The olfactory area is in the roof of the nasal cavity, on the upper septum and superior concha.
- **Olfactory epithelium**: olfactory receptor cells (bipolar neurons with hair-like cilia in the mucus), supporting cells and basal cells.
- The axons pass through the **cribriform plate of the ethmoid** to the **olfactory bulb** — the olfactory nerve (I). A fracture here can cause loss of smell and leakage of cerebrospinal fluid from the nose.

## 5.14 Tongue (organ of taste)

- Muscular organ covered with mucous membrane; front two-thirds in the mouth, back one-third in the oropharynx, separated by a V-shaped groove (sulcus terminalis).
- **Papillae**: filiform (most numerous, no taste buds), fungiform (on the tip and sides, have taste buds), circumvallate (8–12 large ones in a V in front of the sulcus, many taste buds), foliate (sides).
- **Taste buds**: barrel-shaped clusters of gustatory (receptor) and supporting cells opening by a taste pore.
- Nerves of taste: anterior two-thirds — facial nerve (VII) via the chorda tympani; posterior one-third — glossopharyngeal (IX). General sensation, anterior two-thirds — lingual branch of the trigeminal (V). Movement — hypoglossal (XII).

## 5.15 Application and implication in nursing

- **Thyroid surgery**: watch the voice (recurrent laryngeal nerve) and calcium level (parathyroids); keep tracheostomy equipment ready as per policy.
- **Insulin injections** go into the subcutaneous tissue; rotate sites to prevent fatty lumps.
- **Skin**: the epidermis has no blood supply; pressure over bony points cuts off the dermal circulation and causes pressure injury, so reposition patients regularly. Intradermal tests (e.g. Mantoux) go into the dermis.
- **Eye care**: instil drops into the lower conjunctival sac, not on the cornea; press on the inner corner (puncta) after some drops to reduce drainage into the nose.
- **Ear drops and irrigation**: straighten the canal — pull the pinna **up and back in adults**, **down and back in young children**.
- Children's shorter, more horizontal Eustachian tubes explain frequent middle-ear infection.
- Loss of smell or clear nasal discharge after head injury may mean a fracture of the anterior cranial base.

## Remember

- Pituitary sits in the sella turcica; anterior lobe = glandular, posterior lobe = nerve tissue storing ADH and oxytocin.
- Thyroid: 2 lobes + isthmus over tracheal rings 2–4; follicles (T3, T4) and C cells (calcitonin).
- Four parathyroids behind the thyroid.
- Adrenal cortex: glomerulosa, fasciculata, reticularis (salt, sugar, sex); medulla: adrenaline.
- Islets: beta cells (insulin) are the majority.
- Epidermis layers: basale, spinosum, granulosum, lucidum, corneum.
- Eye coats: fibrous (sclera, cornea), vascular (choroid, ciliary body, iris), nervous (retina). Fovea = sharpest vision; optic disc = blind spot.
- Ossicles: malleus, incus, stapes; organ of Corti in the cochlea.
- Taste: VII (anterior 2/3), IX (posterior 1/3).

# Unit 6: The musculoskeletal system

INC Unit VII (10 hours — the biggest unit): the skeletal system (anatomical positions; bones — types, structure, growth and ossification; axial and appendicular skeleton; joints) and the muscular system (types and structure of muscle, muscle groups, principal muscles, and the muscles used in nursing procedures such as injections).

## Part A — The skeletal system

## 6.1 Functions of the skeleton (in brief)

Support and shape, protection of organs (skull, ribs, pelvis), movement (levers for muscles), blood cell formation in red marrow, and storage of calcium and phosphate (and fat in yellow marrow).

## 6.2 Types of bones by shape

| Type | Description | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Long | Longer than wide; shaft and two ends | Femur, humerus, radius, tibia, phalanges |
| Short | Cube-shaped | Carpals, tarsals |
| Flat | Thin, plate-like, often curved | Skull vault bones, sternum, ribs, scapula |
| Irregular | Complex shapes | Vertebrae, facial bones, hip bone |
| Sesamoid | Develop inside a tendon | Patella (largest), pisiform |
| Sutural (Wormian) | Small extra bones in skull sutures | Variable |

## 6.3 Structure of a long bone

```text
        Proximal epiphysis (spongy bone + red marrow, articular cartilage on top)
        ─── epiphyseal plate (growth plate) / line in adults ───
        Metaphysis
        Diaphysis (shaft):  compact bone wall
                            medullary cavity with yellow marrow
                            endosteum lines the cavity
                            periosteum covers the outside
                            nutrient artery enters through the nutrient foramen
        Metaphysis
        Distal epiphysis
```

- **Periosteum**: tough fibrous outer layer with an inner bone-forming (osteogenic) layer; rich in nerves and blood vessels — this is why bone injuries are painful and why the periosteum is needed for healing. It is not present over articular cartilage.
- **Articular cartilage**: hyaline cartilage on joint surfaces.

**Microscopic structure**

- **Compact bone** is built of **osteons (Haversian systems)**: a central (Haversian) canal with vessels and nerves, surrounded by rings (lamellae) of bone matrix; bone cells (**osteocytes**) live in small spaces (lacunae) joined by tiny canals (canaliculi). Volkmann's canals run across, linking the central canals.
- **Spongy (cancellous) bone**: a lattice of thin plates (trabeculae) with red marrow in the spaces; found at bone ends and inside flat and irregular bones.
- **Bone cells**: osteoblasts (build bone), osteocytes (maintain it), osteoclasts (large cells that break bone down and reshape it).
- **Matrix**: about one-third organic (mainly collagen — gives flexibility) and two-thirds inorganic calcium phosphate salts (hydroxyapatite — gives hardness).

## 6.4 Growth and ossification

**Ossification** is the formation of bone.

| Type | Process | Bones |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Intramembranous | Bone forms directly in fibrous membrane | Flat bones of the skull vault, most facial bones, clavicle (partly) |
| Endochondral (intracartilaginous) | A hyaline cartilage model is gradually replaced by bone | Most bones: long bones, vertebrae, base of skull |

**Endochondral ossification of a long bone**

1. A cartilage model of the bone forms in the embryo.
2. A **primary ossification centre** appears in the middle of the shaft; a periosteal collar forms around it.
3. Blood vessels invade; bone replaces cartilage; the medullary cavity forms.
4. **Secondary ossification centres** appear in the epiphyses, mostly after birth.
5. Between the shaft and each epiphysis a plate of cartilage, the **epiphyseal (growth) plate**, keeps growing in length; the shaft side turns into bone.
6. After puberty the plate ossifies completely (the **epiphyseal line**) and growth in length stops.

- **Growth in length**: at the epiphyseal plates.
- **Growth in thickness (width)**: by osteoblasts under the periosteum (appositional growth) while osteoclasts widen the medullary cavity.
- Growth is affected by growth hormone, thyroid hormones, sex hormones, vitamin D, calcium, and weight-bearing exercise. A fracture through the growth plate in a child can affect limb growth.
- **Fontanelles**: membranous gaps in the newborn skull; the **anterior fontanelle** (diamond-shaped) usually closes by about 18 months and the **posterior fontanelle** (triangular) by about 2–3 months (ranges vary).

## 6.5 The skeleton: axial and appendicular

The adult skeleton has **206 bones**: 80 axial and 126 appendicular.

```text
AXIAL (80)                              APPENDICULAR (126)
Skull           22 (8 cranial, 14 facial)  Pectoral girdles  4 (2 clavicles, 2 scapulae)
Ear ossicles     6                         Upper limbs      60 (30 each)
Hyoid            1                         Pelvic girdle     2 (hip bones)
Vertebral column 26                        Lower limbs      60 (30 each)
Thoracic cage   25 (24 ribs + sternum)
```

### Skull

- **Cranial bones (8)**: frontal, 2 parietal, 2 temporal, occipital, sphenoid, ethmoid.
- **Facial bones (14)**: 2 nasal, 2 maxillae, 2 zygomatic, mandible (only movable skull bone), 2 lacrimal, 2 palatine, 2 inferior nasal conchae, vomer.
- **Sutures**: coronal (frontal–parietal), sagittal (between parietals), lambdoid (parietal–occipital), squamous (temporal–parietal).
- **Foramen magnum** in the occipital bone lets the spinal cord pass.

### Vertebral column

| Region | Number | Features |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cervical | 7 | Small bodies; **foramen transversarium** (for vertebral artery); C1 **atlas** (no body, holds the skull), C2 **axis** (dens/odontoid process); C7 vertebra prominens |
| Thoracic | 12 | Facets for ribs; long downward spines |
| Lumbar | 5 | Largest, heavy bodies; short square spines |
| Sacrum | 1 (5 fused) | Joins the hip bones |
| Coccyx | 1 (4 fused, varies) | Tailbone |

- A typical vertebra: **body** in front, **vertebral arch** (pedicles and laminae) behind enclosing the **vertebral foramen**, spinous process, two transverse processes, articular processes. Intervertebral discs (fibrocartilage, with a soft centre — nucleus pulposus) lie between bodies.
- **Curvatures**: cervical and lumbar curves are concave backward (lordosis, secondary); thoracic and sacral curves are convex backward (kyphosis, primary).
- The spinal cord ends at about the **L1–L2** level in adults, so lumbar puncture is done below this, usually at L3–L4 or L4–L5.

### Thoracic cage

Sternum (manubrium, body, xiphoid process), 12 pairs of ribs (1–7 true, 8–10 false, 11–12 floating) and 12 thoracic vertebrae.

### Appendicular skeleton

| Region | Bones |
| --- | --- |
| Pectoral girdle | Clavicle (S-shaped; most commonly fractured bone), scapula (with acromion, coracoid process, glenoid cavity) |
| Arm | Humerus (head, surgical neck, greater and lesser tubercles, medial and lateral epicondyles) |
| Forearm | Radius (lateral, thumb side), ulna (medial; olecranon forms the point of the elbow) |
| Hand | 8 carpals, 5 metacarpals, 14 phalanges |
| Pelvic girdle | Two hip bones (each = ilium + ischium + pubis fused at the **acetabulum**), joined to the sacrum behind and at the symphysis pubis in front |
| Thigh | Femur (longest and strongest bone; head, neck, greater and lesser trochanters, condyles) |
| Knee | Patella |
| Leg | Tibia (medial, weight-bearing; medial malleolus), fibula (lateral; lateral malleolus) |
| Foot | 7 tarsals (talus, calcaneus — heel, navicular, cuboid, 3 cuneiforms), 5 metatarsals, 14 phalanges |

**Female vs male pelvis**: the female pelvis is wider and shallower, with a round (gynaecoid) inlet, a wider subpubic angle (about 90° or more) and a larger outlet — adapted for childbirth.

## 6.6 Joints (articulations)

### Classification

| By structure | By movement | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Fibrous** — bones joined by fibrous tissue | Mostly immovable (synarthrosis) | Skull sutures, tooth sockets (gomphosis), distal tibiofibular joint (syndesmosis, slightly movable) |
| **Cartilaginous** — joined by cartilage | Slightly movable (amphiarthrosis) | Primary (hyaline): epiphyseal plates, 1st rib–sternum. Secondary (fibrocartilage): intervertebral discs, symphysis pubis |
| **Synovial** — joint cavity with fluid | Freely movable (diarthrosis) | Shoulder, elbow, hip, knee |

### Structure of a synovial joint

```text
   Bone ─────────────
   Articular (hyaline) cartilage
   Joint cavity with synovial fluid
   Synovial membrane lining the capsule
   Fibrous capsule, strengthened by ligaments
   Articular cartilage
   Bone ─────────────
   (some joints also have discs/menisci, bursae, fat pads)
```

### Types of synovial joint

| Type | Movement | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ball and socket | All directions, including rotation | Shoulder, hip |
| Hinge | Flexion and extension | Elbow, knee (modified), ankle, interphalangeal |
| Pivot | Rotation around one axis | Atlanto-axial (C1–C2), proximal radio-ulnar |
| Condyloid (ellipsoid) | Flexion–extension, abduction–adduction | Wrist (radiocarpal), metacarpophalangeal |
| Saddle | Like condyloid plus opposition | Carpometacarpal joint of the thumb |
| Gliding (plane) | Sliding | Intercarpal, between vertebral articular processes |

### Major joints

- **Shoulder (glenohumeral)**: ball and socket between the head of the humerus and the shallow glenoid cavity, deepened by the glenoid labrum. Very mobile but unstable; held mainly by the **rotator cuff** muscles (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis). Dislocates easily (usually forward and downward).
- **Elbow**: hinge between humerus, ulna and radius.
- **Hip**: ball and socket between the femoral head and acetabulum; deep socket and strong ligaments make it stable. Fracture of the femoral neck is common in older women with osteoporosis.
- **Knee**: largest joint; modified hinge between femoral condyles, tibia and patella. **Menisci** (medial and lateral, fibrocartilage) cushion it; **cruciate ligaments** (anterior and posterior) inside and **collateral ligaments** (medial and lateral) at the sides give stability.
- **Ankle**: hinge between tibia, fibula and talus.

## Part B — The muscular system

## 6.7 Types and structure of muscle

The three types (skeletal, smooth, cardiac) are compared in Unit 1. Here we look at skeletal muscle in more detail.

```text
Muscle (covered by epimysium)
  → Fascicles (bundles, covered by perimysium)
     → Muscle fibres = muscle cells (covered by endomysium; sarcolemma, many nuclei)
        → Myofibrils
           → Sarcomeres (thin actin and thick myosin filaments) → striations
```

- A muscle is attached to bone by a **tendon** (dense regular connective tissue) or a flat sheet (**aponeurosis**). The fixed end is the **origin**; the moving end is the **insertion**.
- **Motor unit**: one motor neuron and all the muscle fibres it supplies; the **neuromuscular junction** is where the nerve meets the fibre.
- Muscles work in groups: prime mover (agonist), opposing (antagonist), helpers (synergists) and stabilisers (fixators).

## 6.8 Muscle groups

| Region | Important muscles | Main action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Head (face and jaw) | Frontalis, orbicularis oculi (closes eye), orbicularis oris (closes lips), buccinator (cheek), masseter and temporalis (chewing) | Facial expression, chewing |
| Neck | **Sternocleidomastoid** (turns head to the opposite side; accessory muscle of breathing), trapezius (upper part) | Moves head, shrugs shoulders |
| Thorax | External and internal intercostals, diaphragm, pectoralis major and minor, serratus anterior | Breathing, arm movements |
| Abdomen | Rectus abdominis, external oblique, internal oblique, transversus abdominis | Support viscera, flex trunk, forced expiration, raise abdominal pressure (coughing, defaecation, labour) |
| Back | Trapezius, latissimus dorsi, erector spinae | Posture, arm extension |
| Pelvis | Pelvic floor: **levator ani** and coccygeus | Support pelvic organs, control of continence |
| Upper limb | **Deltoid**, biceps brachii, triceps brachii, forearm flexors and extensors | Arm and hand movement |
| Lower limb | **Gluteus maximus, medius and minimus**, quadriceps femoris (**vastus lateralis**, vastus medialis, vastus intermedius, rectus femoris), hamstrings, gastrocnemius and soleus (calf), tibialis anterior | Standing, walking, posture |

## 6.9 Principal muscles

| Muscle | Origin → insertion (simplified) | Action | Nerve |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Deltoid | Clavicle, acromion and spine of scapula → deltoid tuberosity of humerus | Abducts arm (also flexes and extends) | Axillary nerve |
| Biceps brachii | Scapula (two heads) → radial tuberosity | Flexes elbow, supinates forearm | Musculocutaneous nerve |
| Triceps brachii | Scapula and humerus (three heads) → olecranon of ulna | Extends elbow | Radial nerve |
| Diaphragm and intercostals | See Unit 2 | Breathing | Phrenic; intercostal nerves |
| Rectus abdominis | Pubis → xiphoid and costal cartilages 5–7 | Flexes trunk, compresses abdomen | Lower intercostal nerves |
| Levator ani (pelvic floor) | Pubis, fascia, ischial spine → coccyx and midline | Supports pelvic organs, helps continence | Sacral nerves (S2–S4) |
| Gluteus maximus | Ilium, sacrum, coccyx → gluteal tuberosity of femur, iliotibial tract | Extends hip (climbing, rising from sitting) | Inferior gluteal nerve |
| Gluteus medius and minimus | Outer surface of ilium → greater trochanter | Abduct hip; keep pelvis level when walking | Superior gluteal nerve |
| Vastus lateralis | Femur (greater trochanter, linea aspera) → patella and tibial tuberosity (via patellar tendon) | Extends knee | Femoral nerve |

## 6.10 Major muscles involved in nursing procedures (intramuscular injection sites)

| Site | Muscle | How to locate (outline) | Main structure to avoid |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Deltoid | Deltoid | About 2–3 fingerbreadths (roughly 2.5–5 cm) below the acromion, in the middle of the muscle, above the armpit level | Radial nerve and brachial artery lower down; axillary nerve |
| Ventrogluteal | Gluteus medius and minimus | Heel of the hand on the greater trochanter, index finger on the ASIS, middle finger spread along the iliac crest; inject in the centre of the V between the two fingers | Few large nerves or vessels — often preferred |
| Dorsogluteal | Gluteus maximus | Upper outer quadrant of the buttock (divide the buttock into four) | **Sciatic nerve** and superior gluteal vessels — many guidelines now prefer the ventrogluteal site |
| Vastus lateralis | Vastus lateralis | Middle third of the outer front thigh, between the greater trochanter and the knee | Femoral vessels and nerve on the inner thigh |
| Rectus femoris | Rectus femoris | Middle third of the front of the thigh | Used mainly for self-injection |

**Why the vastus lateralis is the usual site in infants**: the gluteal muscles are poorly developed until a child walks, and the sciatic nerve is relatively large and close; the vastus lateralis is thick and away from major vessels and nerves.

**Other procedures using muscle anatomy**

- **Pelvic floor (Kegel) exercises** strengthen the levator ani after childbirth and for stress incontinence.
- **Correct lifting**: use the strong quadriceps and gluteal muscles (bend the knees, keep the back straight) to protect the erector spinae and the lumbar discs.
- **Range-of-motion exercises** move each joint through its normal movements to prevent contractures.
- Turning and positioning protect the skin over bony prominences: sacrum, greater trochanter, heels, elbows, occiput, scapulae, ischial tuberosities.

## 6.11 Application and implication in nursing

- **Fractures**: immobilise the joint above and below; check circulation, sensation and movement distal to plasters and splints (compartment syndrome warning signs).
- **Older adults** lose bone mass (osteoporosis) — fall prevention protects the hip and wrist.
- **Lumbar puncture** positioning (lateral, knees to chest, back arched) opens the spaces between lumbar spines.
- **Fontanelles** are checked in infants: a bulging fontanelle may mean raised intracranial pressure; a sunken one, dehydration.
- **Body mechanics** reduce back injury in nurses.
- **Immobility** causes muscle wasting, joint stiffness and bone loss; early mobilisation and ROM exercises prevent them.

## Remember

- 206 bones: axial 80, appendicular 126.
- Long bone: diaphysis, epiphyses, epiphyseal plate, periosteum, medullary cavity.
- Haversian system = osteon; osteoblasts build, osteoclasts break down.
- Length growth at the epiphyseal plate; width growth under the periosteum.
- Vertebrae: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, sacrum, coccyx; spinal cord ends at L1–L2.
- Hip bone = ilium + ischium + pubis; femur is the longest bone; clavicle is the most fractured.
- Joints: fibrous, cartilaginous, synovial; shoulder and hip are ball and socket; knee is a modified hinge.
- Deltoid — axillary nerve; abducts arm.
- Ventrogluteal site uses gluteus medius; dorsogluteal risks the sciatic nerve; vastus lateralis is the infant site.

# Unit 7: The renal and reproductive systems

This notes file joins **INC Unit VIII, the renal system** (5 hours: kidney, ureters, bladder, urethra) and **INC Unit IX, the reproductive system** (5 hours: male organs, female organs, breast). Urine formation, the menstrual cycle and hormones are in Applied Physiology.

## Part A — The renal (urinary) system

```text
 Kidneys (make urine) → Ureters (carry) → Urinary bladder (stores) → Urethra (passes out)
```

## 7.1 Kidneys: position and relations

- Two bean-shaped organs, each about **11 cm long, 6 cm wide, 3 cm thick**, weighing about 150 g.
- Lie on the posterior abdominal wall, **behind the peritoneum (retroperitoneal)**, on either side of the vertebral column, roughly from **T12 to L3**.
- The **right kidney is a little lower** than the left because the liver lies above it.
- Upper poles touch the diaphragm; the **adrenal glands** sit on top. The lower ribs (11th and 12th) cross the back of the kidneys.
- Relations in front: right kidney — liver, duodenum, hepatic flexure of colon; left kidney — stomach, spleen, pancreas, splenic flexure, jejunum.

**Coverings (inside to outside)**

1. **Renal (fibrous) capsule** — thin, tough, close to the surface.
2. **Perirenal fat (adipose capsule)** — cushions the kidney.
3. **Renal fascia** — holds the kidney and adrenal gland to the posterior wall.
4. Pararenal fat outside the fascia.

## 7.2 Internal structure of the kidney

A cut (coronal) section shows:

```text
       Capsule
  ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │ CORTEX (outer, granular) │
  │   Renal columns dip in   │
  │  ▼ ▼ MEDULLA: pyramids ▼ │
  │   papilla → minor calyx  │
  │   → major calyx          │
  │   → RENAL PELVIS ────────┼──► Ureter
  │   Hilum: renal artery in,│
  │   renal vein out         │
  └──────────────────────────┘
```

- **Cortex**: outer reddish layer containing glomeruli and convoluted tubules.
- **Medulla**: 8–18 cone-shaped **renal pyramids** (striped because of loops of Henle and collecting ducts); their tips (papillae) open into **minor calyces** → **major calyces** (2–3) → **renal pelvis** → ureter.
- **Renal columns**: extensions of cortex between pyramids.
- **Hilum**: notch on the medial border where the renal artery enters and the renal vein, ureter (pelvis), nerves and lymphatics pass.

## 7.3 The nephron

The **nephron** is the structural and functional unit of the kidney; each kidney has about one million.

```text
Afferent arteriole → GLOMERULUS (capillary tuft) → Efferent arteriole → peritubular capillaries
                        inside Bowman's capsule
RENAL CORPUSCLE = Glomerulus + Bowman's (glomerular) capsule
   ↓
Proximal convoluted tubule (cortex; cuboidal cells with brush border)
   ↓
Loop of Henle: descending limb → hairpin bend → ascending limb (dips into medulla)
   ↓
Distal convoluted tubule (cortex; touches its own afferent arteriole at the
                          juxtaglomerular apparatus)
   ↓
Collecting duct (shared by many nephrons) → papilla → minor calyx
```

- **Cortical nephrons** (most) have short loops; **juxtamedullary nephrons** have long loops reaching deep into the medulla (concentrating urine).
- **Juxtaglomerular apparatus**: juxtaglomerular cells in the afferent arteriole wall (secrete renin) plus the macula densa of the distal tubule.
- The **filtration membrane**: glomerular capillary endothelium (with pores), basement membrane, and the podocytes of the inner layer of Bowman's capsule.

**Blood supply**: renal artery (from the abdominal aorta) → segmental → interlobar → arcuate → interlobular arteries → afferent arterioles → glomeruli → efferent arterioles → peritubular capillaries and vasa recta → veins → renal vein → inferior vena cava. The kidneys receive about one-fifth of the cardiac output.

## 7.4 Ureters

- Two muscular tubes about **25–30 cm** long and 3 mm wide, carrying urine from the renal pelvis to the bladder by **peristalsis**.
- Run down on the posterior abdominal wall (on the psoas muscle), cross the pelvic brim near the bifurcation of the common iliac artery, and enter the back of the bladder obliquely.
- Wall: transitional epithelium (mucosa), smooth muscle, fibrous outer coat.
- **Three narrow points**: pelviureteric junction, crossing of the pelvic brim, and entry into the bladder. Kidney stones commonly lodge here and cause colicky pain radiating from loin to groin.
- The oblique passage through the bladder wall acts as a valve preventing backflow.

## 7.5 Urinary bladder

- Hollow muscular sac in the pelvis, behind the symphysis pubis. In females it lies in front of the uterus and vagina; in males in front of the rectum, above the prostate.
- When full it rises into the abdomen and can be felt above the symphysis pubis (a distended bladder in retention).
- Capacity: usually about 400–600 ml in adults; the urge to pass urine is felt at a few hundred ml (figures vary).
- **Wall**: transitional epithelium in folds (rugae) when empty; the **detrusor muscle** (three layers of smooth muscle); outer serous/adventitial coat.
- **Trigone**: smooth triangular area on the inside of the base between the two ureteric openings and the internal urethral opening; it does not stretch. Infection often starts here.
- **Sphincters**: internal urethral sphincter (smooth muscle at the bladder neck, involuntary) and external urethral sphincter (skeletal muscle in the pelvic floor, voluntary).

## 7.6 Urethra

| Feature | Female | Male |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Length | About **4 cm** | About **18–20 cm** |
| Course | Straight, behind the symphysis pubis; opens in the vestibule between the clitoris and vaginal opening | S-shaped; passes through the prostate, pelvic floor and penis |
| Parts | — | Prostatic (about 3 cm, ejaculatory ducts open), membranous (shortest and narrowest, through the external sphincter), spongy/penile (longest, in the corpus spongiosum) |
| Function | Urine only | Urine and semen |

The short female urethra close to the anus explains why urinary tract infections are much more common in women.

## Part B — The reproductive system

## 7.7 Male reproductive organs

```text
 Testis (sperm + testosterone) → Epididymis (stores, matures sperm)
 → Vas (ductus) deferens → joins the duct of the seminal vesicle → Ejaculatory duct
 → through the prostate → Urethra → out through the penis
```

| Organ | Structure |
| --- | --- |
| **Scrotum** | Pouch of skin and dartos muscle outside the body; keeps the testes about 2–3 °C below body temperature, needed for sperm production |
| **Testes** | Two oval glands (about 4–5 cm); covered by the **tunica vaginalis** (outside) and the tough **tunica albuginea**; divided into about 250 lobules containing coiled **seminiferous tubules** (sperm form here from spermatogonia, supported by **Sertoli cells**); **interstitial (Leydig) cells** between the tubules make **testosterone** |
| **Epididymis** | Highly coiled tube (about 6 m uncoiled) on the back of the testis — head, body, tail; sperm mature and are stored |
| **Vas (ductus) deferens** | Muscular tube about 45 cm; travels in the **spermatic cord** (with testicular artery, pampiniform plexus of veins, nerves and lymphatics) through the **inguinal canal** into the pelvis; this is the tube cut in vasectomy |
| **Seminal vesicles** | Two coiled glands behind the bladder; their alkaline fluid with fructose forms most of the semen |
| **Ejaculatory ducts** | Formed by the vas and the seminal vesicle duct; pass through the prostate into the urethra |
| **Prostate gland** | Chestnut-sized gland below the bladder surrounding the first part of the urethra; adds a thin milky fluid; enlarges in older men (benign enlargement) and can obstruct urine flow; felt through the rectum |
| **Bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands** | Pea-sized, below the prostate; mucus for lubrication |
| **Penis** | Root, body and glans; three columns of erectile tissue — two **corpora cavernosa** (upper) and one **corpus spongiosum** (lower, contains the urethra, expands as the glans); foreskin (prepuce) covers the glans |

The testes develop in the abdomen and descend through the inguinal canal into the scrotum before birth; an undescended testis needs attention in the newborn check.

## 7.8 Female reproductive organs

**External genitalia (vulva)**: mons pubis, labia majora, labia minora, clitoris (erectile tissue), vestibule (with urethral and vaginal openings), greater vestibular (Bartholin's) glands, and the perineum (area between the vaginal opening and anus, which may tear in childbirth).

**Internal organs**

```text
         Uterine tube   Fundus   Uterine tube
   Ovary  (fimbriae)  ┌───────┐  (fimbriae)  Ovary
      ○ ~~~~~~~~~~~~~ │ Body  │ ~~~~~~~~~~~~~ ○
                      │Cavity │
                       \ Isthmus /
                        │Cervix│
                        │      │ ← internal os / external os
                        │Vagina│
```

| Organ | Structure |
| --- | --- |
| **Vagina** | Fibromuscular tube about 8–10 cm, from the vestibule up and back to the cervix; lined with stratified squamous non-keratinised epithelium (no glands; acidic secretions protect against infection); the spaces around the cervix are the **fornices** (posterior one deepest) |
| **Uterus** | Hollow, pear-shaped muscular organ, about 7.5 cm long, 5 cm wide, 2.5 cm thick (non-pregnant), between the bladder and rectum; usually **anteverted and anteflexed** (tilted forward). Parts: **fundus** (above the tubes), **body**, **isthmus**, **cervix** (with internal os and external os) |
| Uterine wall | **Endometrium** (mucous lining; functional layer shed in menstruation, basal layer regenerates it), **myometrium** (thick smooth muscle in interlacing layers; contracts in labour and compresses blood vessels after delivery), **perimetrium** (peritoneum) |
| Supports of the uterus | Pelvic floor (levator ani), **transverse cervical (cardinal) ligaments**, uterosacral ligaments, round ligaments (keep it anteverted), broad ligaments (folds of peritoneum, carrying the tubes and vessels); weakness leads to prolapse |
| **Uterine (fallopian) tubes** | About 10 cm each; parts: interstitial (in the uterine wall), isthmus (narrow), **ampulla** (widest; **usual site of fertilisation** and of ectopic pregnancy), infundibulum with finger-like **fimbriae** near the ovary; lined by ciliated columnar epithelium; cilia and peristalsis move the ovum |
| **Ovaries** | Two almond-shaped glands (about 3 × 2 × 1 cm) on each side of the uterus, attached to the broad ligament (mesovarium) and to the uterus (ovarian ligament); outer **cortex** with follicles at various stages and the **corpus luteum**, inner **medulla** with vessels; produce ova, oestrogen and progesterone |

**Blood supply**: uterine artery (from the internal iliac; crosses above the ureter near the cervix — "water under the bridge", important in hysterectomy) and ovarian artery (from the abdominal aorta).

## 7.9 Breast (mammary gland)

- Modified sweat glands lying in the superficial fascia over the **pectoralis major**, from about the 2nd to the 6th rib, from the sternal edge to the mid-axillary line. The **axillary tail** extends into the axilla.
- **Nipple** (with openings of 15–20 lactiferous ducts) surrounded by the pigmented **areola**, which has Montgomery's glands (sebaceous, lubricate during feeding).
- **Glandular tissue**: 15–20 **lobes** arranged like the spokes of a wheel; each lobe has lobules of milk-secreting **alveoli** → ducts → **lactiferous duct**, which widens under the areola (lactiferous sinus) before opening on the nipple.
- **Supporting tissue**: fat (gives size and shape) and fibrous bands — **suspensory (Cooper's) ligaments**. Cancer pulling on these ligaments causes dimpling of the skin.
- **Lymphatic drainage**: about three-quarters to the **axillary lymph nodes**, the rest mainly to internal mammary (parasternal) nodes — so breast cancer often spreads to the axilla first.
- Male breast is rudimentary.

```text
  Chest wall │ Pectoralis major │ fat + lobes ──► ducts ──► sinus ──► nipple
             │                  │   Cooper's ligaments to skin
```

## 7.10 Application and implication in nursing

- **Catheterisation**: the female urethra is short and opens just above the vagina; in males the S-shaped urethra is straightened by holding the penis upward during insertion. Strict asepsis is essential, especially in females.
- **Bladder assessment**: a palpable bladder above the pubis suggests retention; record intake and output.
- **Renal angle**: tenderness at the angle between the 12th rib and the spine (loin) suggests kidney infection.
- **Kidney biopsy and nephrostomy** depend on the kidney's position behind the lower ribs.
- **Perineal care** from front to back reduces urinary infection in females.
- **Breast self-examination** covers the whole breast including the axillary tail; women should know their normal breast and report lumps, dimpling or nipple changes.
- **Antenatal and postnatal care** depend on knowing the uterus (fundal height), cervix and pelvic floor; pelvic floor exercises reduce prolapse and incontinence.
- **Testicular self-examination** helps detect lumps early in young men.

## Remember

- Kidneys: retroperitoneal, T12–L3, right lower than left; capsule, perirenal fat, renal fascia.
- Cortex (glomeruli, convoluted tubules); medulla (pyramids).
- Nephron: glomerulus + Bowman's capsule → PCT → loop of Henle → DCT → collecting duct.
- Ureter 25–30 cm, three narrow points; bladder trigone; detrusor muscle.
- Urethra: female 4 cm; male 18–20 cm (prostatic, membranous, spongy).
- Testis: seminiferous tubules (sperm), Leydig cells (testosterone).
- Path of sperm: testis → epididymis → vas deferens → ejaculatory duct → urethra.
- Uterus: fundus, body, isthmus, cervix; endometrium, myometrium, perimetrium; anteverted, anteflexed.
- Fertilisation usually in the ampulla of the uterine tube.
- Breast: 15–20 lobes, lactiferous ducts, Cooper's ligaments; most lymph to axillary nodes.
